summary: Defines the PPP encapsulation scheme for carrying multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links, together with the Link Control Protocol, an extensible way to negotiate link options. It was replaced by RFC 1548.

plainLanguage.summary: PPP is the set of rules for talking over a cable between two computers. It defines how a packet is framed for the wire, how the two ends negotiate settings such as the maximum packet size, and how the link is started, authenticated and shut down.

questions: what is the link control protocol
what is the ppp frame format
subtitle: How two hosts at the ends of a serial line agree on how to carry IP, and how the link is set up and torn down.

tldr.problem: Almost every host has a serial port, but there was no agreed way to carry IP datagrams over one. Each site invented its own framing, so equipment could not talk to equipment.
tldr.mechanism: PPP provides three things: an encapsulation that puts datagrams into frames based on HDLC, a Link Control Protocol that negotiates the link's options and manages its life cycle, and a family of Network Control Protocols that configure each network-layer protocol separately.
tldr.outcome: Any two hosts can bring up a link, agree on its settings without an operator, and then carry IP. The document has been replaced by RFC 1548.

today: RFC 1331 was a Proposed Standard published in May 1992. It obsoleted RFC 1171 and RFC 1172, and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 1548, which is the current specification of the Point-to-Point Protocol.

sections.title: Why PPP and Its Three Parts
sections.content:
In the last few years the Internet has seen explosive growth in the number of hosts supporting TCP/IP. The vast majority of these hosts are connected to Local Area Networks of various types, Ethernet being the most common. Most of the other hosts are connected through Wide Area Networks such as X.25 style Public Data Networks. Relatively few are connected with simple point-to-point, that is serial, links, yet point-to-point links are among the oldest methods of data communications and almost every host supports them: asynchronous RS-232-C interfaces are essentially ubiquitous.

One reason for the small number of point-to-point IP links is the lack of a standard encapsulation protocol. There are plenty of non-standard encapsulation protocols available, but not one which has been agreed upon as an Internet Standard. By contrast, standard encapsulation schemes do exist for the transmission of datagrams over most popular LANs. PPP provides an encapsulation protocol over both bit-oriented synchronous links and asynchronous links with 8 bits of data and no parity; these links MUST be full-duplex, but MAY be either dedicated or circuit-switched. PPP uses HDLC as a basis for the encapsulation.

PPP has been carefully designed to retain compatibility with most commonly used supporting hardware. An escape mechanism is specified to allow control data such as XON/XOFF to be transmitted transparently over the link and to remove spurious control data which may be injected into the link by intervening hardware and software. The encapsulation also provides for multiplexing of different network-layer protocols simultaneously over the same link, and by default only 8 additional octets are necessary to form the encapsulation, though in environments where bandwidth is at a premium it may be shortened to as few as 2 octets.

More importantly, PPP provides a Link Control Protocol. The LCP is used to automatically agree upon the encapsulation format options, handle varying limits on sizes of packets, authenticate the identity of its peer on the link, determine when a link is functioning properly and when it is defunct, detect a looped-back link and other common misconfiguration errors, and terminate the link. A family of Network Control Protocols then handles the specific needs of each network-layer protocol, such as the assignment and management of IP addresses, which is especially difficult over circuit-switched point-to-point links such as dial-up modem servers.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP has three jobs: framing the packets, agreeing on how the link should behave, and then configuring each network protocol, such as IP, once the link is up.

sections.title: The PPP Frame Format
sections.content:
PPP uses the principles, terminology and frame structure of the ISO High-level Data Link Control procedures, as modified by the ISO addendum on start/stop transmission. The PPP frame structure is also consistent with CCITT Recommendation X.25 LAPB, since that too is based on HDLC.

A frame begins with a Flag Sequence, a single octet with the binary sequence 01111110, hexadecimal 0x7e, which indicates the beginning or end of a frame. Only one Flag is required between two frames, and two consecutive Flags constitute an empty frame, which is ignored.

The Address field is a single octet containing the binary sequence 11111111, hexadecimal 0xff, the All-Stations address: PPP does not assign individual station addresses. The Control field is a single octet containing 00000011, hexadecimal 0x03, the Unnumbered Information command with the P/F bit set to zero. The Protocol field is two octets and its value identifies the protocol encapsulated in the Information field. All Protocols MUST be odd, the least significant bit of the least significant octet must equal 1, and the least significant bit of the most significant octet must equal 0. Values in the range 0021 to 003f identify the network-layer protocol of specific datagrams, such as 0021 for Internet Protocol, while values in the range c021 and above identify link-layer control protocols such as LCP.

The Information field is zero or more octets and contains the datagram for the protocol specified in the Protocol field. Its end is found by locating the closing Flag Sequence and allowing two octets for the Frame Check Sequence field. The default maximum length of the Information field is 1500 octets, and by negotiation consenting implementations may use other values. The Frame Check Sequence field is normally 16 bits and is calculated over all bits of the Address, Control, Protocol and Information fields, excluding any start and stop bits and any bits or octets inserted for transparency.
sections.plainLanguage: A PPP frame is a flag, a fixed address and control byte, a two-byte number saying which protocol is inside, the payload, and a checksum. The flag value 0x7e marks both the start and the end of a frame.

sections.title: The Link Phases
sections.content:
In order to establish communications over a point-to-point link, each end of the PPP link must first send LCP packets to configure and test the data link. After the link has been established, the peer may be authenticated. Then PPP must send NCP packets to choose and configure one or more network-layer protocols. Once each of the chosen network-layer protocols has been configured, datagrams from each can be sent over the link. The link remains configured until explicit LCP or NCP packets close it down, or until some external event occurs such as an inactivity timer expiring.

The link goes through several distinct phases. In the Link Dead phase the physical layer is not ready; the LCP automaton is in the Initial or Starting states, and the transition to the next phase signals an Up event.

In the Link Establishment phase the Link Control Protocol establishes the connection through an exchange of Configure packets. The exchange is complete, and the LCP Opened state entered, once a Configure-Ack packet has been both sent and received. Any non-LCP packets received during this phase MUST be silently discarded. All Configuration Options are assumed to be at default values unless altered by the configuration exchange, and only options which are independent of particular network-layer protocols are configured by LCP.

In the Authentication phase, which may be desirable on some links, a peer may be required to authenticate itself before network-layer protocol packets are exchanged. By default authentication is not necessary, but if an implementation requires a specific authentication protocol it MUST negotiate it during the Link Establishment phase. Advancement to the Network-Layer Protocol phase MUST NOT occur until the peer is successfully authenticated, and in the event of failure PPP SHOULD proceed instead to the Link Termination phase.

In the Network-Layer Protocol phase each network-layer protocol, such as IP, MUST be separately configured by the appropriate Network Control Protocol, and each NCP may be Opened and Closed at any time. After a NCP has reached the Opened state PPP will carry the corresponding network-layer protocol packets, and any such packets received when the NCP is not Opened SHOULD be silently discarded. In the Link Termination phase, LCP closes the link through an exchange of Terminate packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The link has a life cycle: dead, being set up, being authenticated, carrying traffic, and being shut down. Each end moves through the same phases in step with the other.

sections.title: The Option Negotiation Automaton
sections.content:
The finite-state automaton is defined by events, actions and state transitions. Events include reception of external commands such as Open and Close, expiration of the Restart timer, and reception of packets from a peer. Actions include the starting of the Restart timer and transmission of packets to the peer.

Some types of packets are not differentiated in the automaton descriptions. Configure-Naks and Configure-Rejects, or Code-Rejects and Protocol-Rejects, or Echo-Requests, Echo-Replies and Discard-Requests, do indeed serve different functions, but they always cause the same transitions.

The simplified state diagram describes the sequence of events for reaching agreement on Configuration Options, which is opening the PPP link, and for later termination of the link. The state machine is initially in the Closed state. Once the Opened state has been reached, both ends of the link have met the requirement of having both sent and received a Configure-Ack packet. From Closed, an Open event moves the machine to Req-Sent; from there a good Configure-Request moves it to Ack-Rcvd and a bad one to Req-Sent; from Ack-Rcvd a Configure-Ack moves it to Opened, and from Opened a Close event moves it to Closing and then to Closed.

The document states that the simplified diagram is not a complete representation of the automaton, and that implementation MUST be done by consulting the actual state transition table. It explains why: in previous versions a simplified non-deterministic finite-state automaton was used, with considerable detailed information specified in the semantics, and this led to interoperability problems from differing interpretations. A later addition was a link quality determination protocol, which is referred to in the packet formats as the Quality-Protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends run the same small state machine. Each proposes settings, the other accepts or corrects them, and when both have accepted, the link is open.

sections.title: The LCP Packets
sections.content:
There are three classes of LCP packets. Link Configuration packets are used to establish and configure a link: Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak and Configure-Reject. Link Termination packets are used to terminate a link: Terminate-Request and Terminate-Ack. Link Maintenance packets are used to manage and debug a link: Code-Reject, Protocol-Reject, Echo-Request, Echo-Reply and Discard-Request.

An LCP packet has a Code field of one octet identifying the kind of packet, an Identifier field of one octet that aids in matching requests and replies, a Length field of two octets giving the length of the LCP packet including the Code, Identifier, Length and Data fields, and a Data field of zero or more octets whose format is determined by the Code field. The assigned Code values are 1 Configure-Request, 2 Configure-Ack, 3 Configure-Nak, 4 Configure-Reject, 5 Terminate-Request, 6 Terminate-Ack, 7 Code-Reject, 8 Protocol-Reject, 9 Echo-Request, 10 Echo-Reply, 11 Discard-Request and 12 reserved.

A LCP implementation wishing to open a connection MUST transmit a packet with the Code field set to 1 and the Options field filled with any desired changes to the default link Configuration Options. The Identifier field SHOULD be changed on each transmission, and on reception it should be copied into the Identifier field of the appropriate reply packet. All Configuration Options are always negotiated simultaneously.

This document describes Version 1 of the Link Control Protocol. In the interest of simplicity there is no version field in the LCP packet; if a new version is needed the intention is that a new Data Link Layer Protocol field value will be used to differentiate it. Exactly one Link Control Protocol packet is encapsulated in the Information field of PPP Data Link Layer frames where the Protocol field indicates type hex c021. Regardless of which Configuration Options are enabled, all LCP Link Configuration, Link Termination and Code-Reject packets, codes 1 through 7, are always sent in the full, standard form, so that Configure-Request packets are always recognizable even when one end of the link mistakenly believes the link to be open.
sections.plainLanguage: LCP has eleven message types: four for setting the link up, two for taking it down, and five for testing and diagnosing it. Every one carries a type, a matching number and a length.

sections.title: The Configuration Options
sections.content:
A Configuration Option has a Type field of one octet, a Length field of one octet giving the length of the option including the Type, Length and Data fields, and a Data field of zero or more octets whose format and length are determined by the Type and Length fields. The assigned types are 1 Maximum-Receive-Unit, 2 Async-Control-Character-Map, 3 Authentication-Protocol, 4 Quality-Protocol, 5 Magic-Number, 6 RESERVED, 7 Protocol-Field-Compression and 8 Address-and-Control-Field-Compression.

The Maximum-Receive-Unit option tells the peer that the implementation can receive larger frames, or asks the peer to send smaller frames. If smaller frames are requested, an implementation MUST still be able to receive 1500 octet frames in case link synchronization is lost. The Maximum-Receive-Unit field is two octets and covers only the Data Link Layer Information field: it does not include the header, padding, FCS, or any transparency bits or bytes. The default is 1500.

The Async-Control-Character-Map option allows control characters to be remapped so that the link can be used with hardware that treats certain characters specially. The Authentication-Protocol option names the protocol the peer should use to authenticate itself. The Quality-Protocol option selects the link quality protocol to use. The Magic-Number option detects a looped-back link and helps to detect that the other end is alive. Protocol-Field-Compression and Address-and-Control-Field-Compression allow the two fixed header fields to be shortened on the wire, which is why the RFC notes that the encapsulation may be shortened to as few as 2 octets in environments where bandwidth is at a premium.

The memo's Security Considerations section says only that security issues are briefly discussed in the sections concerning the Authentication Phase and the Authentication-Protocol Configuration Option, and that further discussion is planned in a separate document entitled PPP Authentication Protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The options are the knobs the two ends turn together: the largest frame each will take, how to handle control characters, which authentication protocol to use, and how to detect a cable plugged into itself.

items.label: Configure-Request
items.desc: Proposes the configuration options the sender wants.

items.label: Configure-Ack
items.desc: Accepts the options in the request.

items.label: Configure-Nak
items.desc: Suggests different values for the options.

items.label: Configure-Reject
items.desc: Refuses options that cannot be negotiated.

items.label: Echo-Request
items.desc: Tests that the link is still working.

items.label: Discard-Request
items.desc: Tests the link by asking for the packet to be dropped.
